ABSTRACT: Chiral organophosphorous compounds are very important in catalysis, organic syntheses, and medicinal chemistry.
However, catalytic enantioselective protocols for the axially chiral allenyl phosphorus compounds have never been reported. Herein,
a palladium-catalyzed enantioselective carbon−phosphorus bond formation reaction affording axially chiral allenyl phosphonates has
been developed. The reaction enjoys high yields and ees accommodating a wide range of functional groups. Mechanistic studies have
unveiled an overwhelming kinetic resolution process.
C
hiral biaryls
1
and allenes
2,3
are two very common classes
of most important axially chiral compounds. Biaryl
bisphosphines have been extensively applied as ligands and
catalysts for asymmetric syntheses.
4
In addition, although
commonly used as Lewis bases,
5
some examples of biaryl
bisphosphine oxides have also been reported as ligands in
transition metal-catalyzed coupling reactions (Scheme 1a,
left).
6
However, reports on axially chiral allenyl phosphorus
compounds are very limited (Scheme 1a, right). Ready and co-
workers had identified axially chiral allenylphosphines as
ligands and catalysts for asymmetric syntheses.
7,8
So far,
there has been no report on catalytic asymmetric synthesis of
axially chiral allenyl phosphorus compounds.
9−11
The envi-
sioned challenge is the tautomeric equilibrium between the
pentavalent (RO)
2
P(O)H and trivalent (RO)
2
POH, which
may coordinate overwhelmingly with the catalytic amount of
the palladium in the chiral Pd catalyst with a chiral ligand,
inhibiting the reaction and/or excluding chiral induction
(Scheme 1b, bottom left).
12
In addition, the regioselectivity
of allenylic vs propargylic phosphonates is also an issue
(Scheme 1b, top).
13
We initiated our study on the reaction of racemic 1-
phenylhept-2-ynyl benzoate 1a with diethyl phosphite 2a. After
tedious optimization, it was observed that the reaction worked
best by using Pd

as the catalyst. A variety of
commercially available ligands were examined with THF at 70
°C (Table 1). The reaction with axially chiral biaryls L1−L7 as
ligands afforded the allenylic products (R)-3aa in 24−92%
yields; however, the enantioselectivity was only 24%. Switching
the ligand to SKP (L8)
14
and SDP (L9)
15

L10 with planar chirality, L11 and L12 with central chirality,
L13 and L14 with planar and central chirality, and Sadphos
(L15−L17)
16
with central chirality, the ees were still low. We
were pleased to find that the desired allenyl phosphonate (R)-
3aa was obtained in 69% yield with 86% ee when (R,R)-
DACH-Phenyl Trost ligand (L18)
17
was used as the ligand.
Thus, a series of such Trost ligands with chiral diamine
skeletons, L19−L21, were tested; however, no better result
was observed. We were happy to see that excellent
regioselectivity was achieved in these Pd-catalyzed coupling
reactions without the undesired propargylic product being
formed.

With the optimized conditions in hand (Table 3, entry 14),
we next explored the scope of H-phosphonates (Scheme 2).
When diethyl phosphite (2a) and dimethyl phosphite (2b)
were used, the corresponding allenyl phosphonates (R)-3aa
and (R)-3ab were obtained in decent yields and excellent ees.
Dialkyl phosphites with longer alkyl chains also afforded the
desired products (R)-3ac−(R)-3ae with excellent ees, but the
yields were lower. No products were formed with diisopropyl
phosphite (1f) and diphenyl phosphite (1g). The reaction of
the 5-membered cyclic phosphite, 4,4,5,5-tetramethyl-1,3,2-
dioxaphospholane 2-oxide (2h), with 1a afforded (R)-3ah in
39% yield with 88% ee in MTBE. Delightfully, allenyl
phosphonate (R)-3ai was obtained in 93% yield with 92%
ee, and an s factor
18

dimethyl-1,3,2-dioxaphosphorinan-2-one 2i was applied at
room temperature with THF as solvent.

electron-withdrawing substituents (1e-1k) all performed well
under the standard conditions, giving the corresponding
products (R)-3bi−(R)-3ki in good yields and with excellent
enantioselectivities. 1-(Naphthyl)hept-2-ynyl benzoate (1l)
also worked smoothly under the optimal conditions, forming

were examined, providing the corresponding products (R)-3

Furthermore, propargylic benzoates bearing different alkyl
group (R) groups with halogen (1q), allyl (1t), alkynyl (1u),
cyano (1v), TBS-protected (TBS = tert-butyldimethylsilyl)
alcohol (1w and 1x), indole (1y), and carbazole (1z) were all
compatible under the standard reaction conditions, which
provide a handle for further transformations. The R group may
also be an aryl group, giving the corresponding products (R)-
5ai−(R)-5di. When the propargylic position was substituted
with an alkyl group such as n-Pr, no desired allenyl
phosphonate 5ei was formed. Late-stage modification of
bioactive complexes and pharmaceuticals such as cholesterol
and adapalene derivatives afforded the corresponding allenes
(R)-3aai and (R)-3bbi in good yields and excellent ee. The
absolute configurations of the products were determined by
single-crystal X-ray diffraction of (R)-3hi and (R)-5ci.
To unveil the reaction mechanism, the following experi-
ments were conducted. First, the profile of the ee of the
recovered (R)-1x and the product (R)-3xi vs time indicated
that the reaction is of kinetic resolution (Scheme 4a). In
addition, first-order dependence was observed for the catalyst
obviously (Scheme 4b), and a linear relationship was observed
between the ee of L18 and product (R)-3xi at 5 or 40 min

In summary, we have presented the first example of catalytic
asymmetric allenyl C−P bond formation reactions producing
axially chiral allenylphosphonates from readily available
propargylic benzoates. These products provide an efficient
access to many synthetically and biologically useful phosphorus
compounds. Mechanistic studies unveiled a kinetic resolution
pathway. Further studies of related reactions are currently
ongoing in our laboratory.
